title: The AI reckoning in UX was 20 years in the making
text:
The AI reckoning in UX was 20 years in the making

Everyone thinks AI is coming for design. The truth is uglier and older. The field has done this to itself twice before, and it’s about to do it again.

The UX job market right now is genuinely grim.

Jeff Sauro, PhD and Jim Lewis, PhD found that UX job postings are down 71 percent from their 2022 peak, and research postings are down even further. They also found that one in three organizations cut UX staff in a single year, the worst reading on record, worse than the one right after the 2008 financial crisis.

When companies trimmed their teams, UX roles took a bigger share of the cuts than their headcount would predict. Open your feed on any given day and someone talented is announcing they’re leaving the field, or asking if they should.

The excuse used to explain it is that AI came for us. The tools got good, the machines can design now, and a generation of designers is being automated out of a job they’ve spent their careers training for. In the more than 120 articles and discussions from the UX community that Prakash Shukla and his colleagues analyzed, they found that the automation anxiety, the fear of being de-skilled and replaced, ran through all of it.

Let’s cut the crap. This exact same thing has happened twice before.

What’s happening to UX is real, and it’s painful, but it is not the story people think it is. This is the third time the field has blown up, pulled in a flood of people chasing a hot job, and then contracted hard and squeezed a lot of them back out.

It happened when the dot-com bubble burst. It happened again when the bootcamps turned “UX designer” into a twelve-week certificate. And it’s happening now. AI is only the latest version of a test the field keeps failing to prepare people for, and the most efficient one yet.

AI democratized output, but it did not do the same for expertise, and producing something has never been the same as knowing whether it’s any good. The same point, aimed at our own profession, gets far less flattering when you truly examine it up close.

The uncomfortable truth underneath this reckoning is that the industry spent twenty years teaching an enormous number of people that design is how something looks, and now we live in a reality where AI is very, very good at making things look finished.

Before everyone agrees the robots did this, though, it’s worth being honest about who actually built the thing the robots are now exposing.

We have done this exactly twice before

In the dot-com bust, I sat front and center watching the bloodbath, and while a lot of us saw it coming, it was not a pretty sight.

In the late nineties, the web was the gold rush, and “information architect,” which is what we called UX designers then, the person responsible for how a product actually works and how someone moves through it, not just how it looks, was suddenly a job you could get paid absurd money to do.

The big interactive agencies were hiring anyone who could spell HTML. The one I worked at was part of a wave of consultancies that got enormous by swallowing other agencies, and the whole industry was copying each other by hiring fast, billing faster, and not asking too many questions about whether the people flooding in actually knew the craft.

Why would they? The money was real and the work was getting shipped.

Then the bubble burst. The agencies that had ballooned on hype collapsed in spectacular fashion, and the layoffs were brutal and everywhere. At twenty-five years old, I witnessed a lot of people lose those jobs and felt something close to relief. A bunch of them, I told myself, were never really designers. They’d shown up for the money, they couldn’t do the actual work, and the crash was just sorting that out.

I was half right, and wholly a jerk.

The part I had right is that a boom really does pull in a lot of people who can’t yet do the actual job, which was never making the screens but knowing which ones were right and why. The part I had wrong is that it wasn’t their fault, and losing your livelihood is not a moral verdict on your talent. The pattern was real, however, and it would happen all over again soon enough.

The second time was the bootcamps. Starting around the early twenty-tens, a whole industry sprang up promising to turn anyone into a UX designer in a matter of weeks. It grew at a staggering rate, by one count the coding and design bootcamp industry grew 138 percent in a single year, minting tens of thousands of graduates and turning into a nine-figure business almost overnight.

The pitch came across as irresistible.

Twelve weeks to a certificate, a portfolio, and a six-figure job.

Schools advertised that the overwhelming majority of their students were placed within ninety days.

For a while, during the zero-interest-rate boom, companies were hiring designers as fast as they could find them, and it mostly worked. Graduates really were getting hired.

Then it didn’t.

When the market tightened, the same bootcamps started laying off their own staff, pausing programs, and in some cases shutting down entirely. The graduates they’d minted were suddenly competing for a shrinking number of junior roles against laid-off veterans, and a twelve-week certificate turned out to be useless protection as the tide went out.

None of this was a secret while it was happening. In the middle of the bootcamp boom, there was dissonance in the UX community that the model was broken, that teaching UX in a few weeks produced people who had the vocabulary but not the judgment, that hiring off certificates and portfolios was selecting for exactly the wrong thing, and that when the tools inevitably changed, the fundamentals, such as research, information architecture, and knowing why a layout works, that the fast track skipped, would be the only thing that still mattered.

The warnings were right in our faces, but the industry kept hiring off cheap and inexperienced portfolios anyway.

The thread connecting both waves has nothing to do with the people necessarily being bad at the job (though some arguably were).

Twice now, a hot field pulled in a flood of people and sold them the same bill of goods, that there was a fast, almost effortless way into UX, and a golden ticket waiting at the end of it. And twice now, when the correction came, those were the people it took first.

This wasn’t because they were frauds, but the reality they’d been swindled into was the version a downturn could most easily do without.

This brings us to the third wave, and to the uncomfortable question of what, exactly, the field has been teaching people design is.

What we taught people design was

There’s some real data on the problem that the field actually taught all those people who rushed in.

When Figma surveyed designers for its State of the Designer report, it asked them to define “craft,” you know, what we call the heart of what gives us passion for what we do and what creates great design.

The most common answer, from 58 percent of them, was visual polish. How it looks. Far fewer named the things that actually make a product work, like solving the real problem, understanding the person using it, the judgment to know what matters.

That’s bananas.

This is the tool company’s own data, drawn from its own users, and a majority of the profession defines its core skill as decoration.

That is not an accident, and it is not those “designers’” fault. It’s what they were taught, hired for, and ultimately rewarded for. The bootcamps that minted them sold a promise that you could learn the tools, the layouts, the components, the whole job, in twelve weeks, and come out a seasoned professional.

What twelve weeks can’t teach, which should have been obvious, is the years of watching real people struggle with real products that judgment actually comes from.

Sarah Doody, who has coached designers through their careers for two decades, sees the result constantly, and it isn’t limited to juniors. She describes experienced designers, people with a decade or more on their résumés, who still can’t build a layout with a clear hierarchy or walk into a room and ask the business question that actually matters.

Patrick Neeman has argued for years that the real value has always been in the strategic thinking the production was standing in for. For a long time, that didn’t cost anyone anything, because the job was mostly making screens. You could make things look finished all day, and nobody ever made you prove you knew why.

Things changed though. Google’s UX certificate, with more than 1.5 million enrollments, has become one of the most common ways people now enter the field, and it teaches the software and the deliverables, because that’s what fits in a syllabus, while quietly skipping the part that takes years.

Knowing whether the work is any good is the one thing you can’t shortcut, and the one thing nobody teaches.

This is where we are today, and it’s why this wave hits harder than the last two. A whole generation got taught that design is how something looks, and all of a sudden that’s exactly what AI does well.

Every wave runs the same test, and AI grades harder

Both of those crashes went after the same people. The ones who could only do the production. In the dot-com bust it was offshore shops and templated sites that made them replaceable. With the bootcamps it was simpler, the ones who only ever learned the software, without true strategic chops, couldn’t do anything the market still needed.

Now it’s AI, and it’s the most brutal one yet, because the one thing it’s genuinely great at is creating what appears to be a polished, ready-to-hand-over deliverable.

Ask Milli Vanilli how that works out. The act looked flawless right up until they had to sing live, and then reality hit. The backing track skipped and their whole veneer fell apart in front of everybody.

The split even shows up in the government’s own numbers. In their 2024 to 2034 projections, Michael Rieley and Javier Colato expect graphic design, the part of the field that’s mostly about how things look, to grow about 2 percent over the decade. Nearly flat, 457th out of 832 occupations they tracked. They name it directly as one of the jobs generative AI is already dampening.

Meanwhile the computer and mathematical work, the problem-solving side, is projected to grow 10 percent, and five of the fifteen fastest-growing occupations in the country, data scientists, information security analysts, and research scientists among them, sit in that group.

If you put those two numbers next to each other, the field is actually splitting.

AI does the good-looking part, the clean mockups and slick screens, well enough and cheap enough now that nobody pays a person just to do that.

This is why the survivors of this wave look so different from the casualties. The designers keeping their jobs are the ones who can walk into a review and say they figured out the team was solving the wrong problem, or that a change they fought for moved retention, in numbers, for a reason they can explain.

The people deciding who gets cut aren’t opening your Figma files to admire them. They’re asking what you actually changed about the business, and a lot of beautiful portfolios have no answer. Alex Williams makes the case that the designers who stay are the ones who can show their work moved a real number, conversion, retention, support load, in language a CFO reads fluently.

None of that is a life sentence, at least not yet. The dividing line AI is drawing runs between people who were taught to produce and people who learned to think. That line leans toward the idea that the thinking can be learned by anyone willing to do the unglamorous work.

Perhaps, this is what the field should have been teaching the whole time.

The fundamentals were always the job

It would be easy to end this by blaming AI, but that’s ignorant and wrong.

AI didn’t do any of this. It didn’t sell a twelve-week path to a career, hire designers for their dribbble shots, or build a cottage industry of certificates for tools instead of courses in how people think. Our industry did all of that, over twenty years, and AI is just the new guy coming in trying to be as helpful as possible.

Being angry at the tool is like being angry at the alarm clock.

The thing to take from this is not despair, because the numbers don’t support despair.

The work isn’t going away. It’s merely sorting itself out and the part of design that was always decoration is flattening out, the part that was always about thinking is still growing.

Kate Moran, Raluca Budiu, and Sarah Gibbons state that the fundamentals of good design don’t change, but the stakes are rising, and the people who thrive will be the ones who treat UX as strategic problem solving instead of a pile of deliverables.

Once again, design is being asked to prove it was ever more than decoration.

Even Jakob Nielsen, who helped invent this field, lands in the same place. Once AI handles execution, he argues, the whole bottleneck moves to judgment, and the only people who should feel threatened are the ones who defined their skills narrowly and low.

AI is a threat in exact proportion to how little thinking your job required.

If you’re wondering whether that certificate on your LinkedIn is worth the time, it isn’t. The UX Design Institute’s State of UX Hiring report, built on more than 500 hiring managers and practitioners, found that what gets you hired is the portfolio and the thinking you can show, not the credential you collected. A certificate can teach you the tool, but so can a YouTube video. Bootcamps can’t teach you whether what you made with any tools is actually good or smart, and that is what matters to the best people hiring in the industry.

What a certificate and AI can’t do for you is clear direction. You, a human, need to be able to look at the research, the problem, the half-built thing in front of you, and say strategically where it should go and why.

Jessica S. Hall tells designers to stop taking orders. Take what’s in front of you, figure out what the problem actually is, and propose a way forward instead of waiting to be handed one. The ones who get cut are usually the ones still waiting for the brief.

The work that survives is the oldest and least glamorous stuff in the field. Understanding the person you’re designing for. Knowing why one layout guides someone and another loses them.

Walking into a room full of executives and connecting a design decision to something the business actually cares about. Christine Haskell has written that in every one of these shifts, production gets easier while judgment gets more valuable, and that the craft was never reducible to the techniques a tool can now copy.

Sarah Doody keeps hammering the same thing: the designers who last never stopped developing their own judgment and refused to let a tool think for them. None of it is new. It’s what the best designers were always doing, and it survives every one of these waves because it’s the part no tool has learned to fake.

I say “we” through all of this on purpose, because I’m part of the field that let it happen, and twenty-five-year-old me, who felt relief watching people lose their jobs had plenty to learn too.

Whether you like it or not, the point of saying it out loud is to be honest that we built a version of this profession that was always going to get a bill, and to push, loudly, back toward the fundamentals that would have protected people in the first place.

For over twenty years, the field did a remarkable impression of the emperor’s new clothes. Everyone agreed the work was magnificent and nobody wanted to be the one to say a lot of it was decoration over nothing, and the longer it went on, the more expensive it got to admit.

AI is just the kid in the crowd saying the obvious thing out loud.

Every one of these waves clears out the same thing, and it does hurt. It’s the people who were sold decoration and told it was design. And every one keeps the same thing: the people who can actually do the work. AI is only frightening if what you were trained to sell was how it looks. If you learned how to think, it’s a very fast assistant.

The fundamentals were always the job. They still are. The sooner the field admits it taught people otherwise, the sooner it can start teaching them right.

References and further reading

The reckoning

  • Jeff Sauro and Jim Lewis, How Does the UX Job Market Look? (MeasuringU). The hard numbers behind the downturn: UX postings down 71 percent from their peak, and one in three organizations cutting UX staff in a single year.
  • UX Design Jobs and AI Displacement (Jobs After AI). On how UX roles took a larger share of cuts than their headcount would predict.
  • Prakash Shukla and colleagues, De-skilling, Cognitive Offloading, and Misplaced Responsibilities (arXiv). An analysis of more than 120 UX community articles and discussions, finding automation anxiety running through all of it.

We have done this before

  • The Last Big Tech Layoff Bloodbath: the Dot-Com Bust of 2000–2001 (SFist). A retrospective on the crash that cleared out the first wave.
  • Don Norman and Jakob Nielsen, The Definition of User Experience (Nielsen Norman Group). The original definition of UX from the people who coined the term.
  • The MarchFirst Autopsy (Unicorn Burn). How the dot-com roll-up giants grew huge and collapsed.
  • Coding Bootcamp Market Data (Course Report). The bootcamp boom, including the 138 percent single-year growth.
  • Coding Bootcamp Outcomes (SwitchUp). Placement data from the boom years, when graduates really were getting hired.
  • Bootcamps Are Dying (Datastream). The collapse: bootcamps laying off staff, pausing programs, and shutting down.
  • UX Design (Interaction Design Foundation). A reference on the fundamentals the fast track skips.
  • CFPB Takes Action Against BloomTech (Consumer Financial Protection Bureau). The federal action against a flagship bootcamp for misrepresenting its placement rates.

What the field taught

  • State of the Designer (Figma). The survey in which 58 percent of designers defined craft as visual polish.
  • Sarah Doody (Career Strategy Lab). On experienced designers who never built the judgment underneath the polish.
  • Patrick Neeman, What UX Competencies in a Generative AI World Could Look Like. On moving from pixel-pushing to strategic thinking.
  • Google UX Design Certificate (Coursera). The 1.5-million-enrollment credential that teaches the software and skips the years.

Every wave runs the same test

  • The Rise and Fall of Milli Vanilli (CBC). The act that looked flawless until the track skipped live.
  • Michael Rieley and Javier Colato, Industry and Occupational Employment Projections, 2024–34 (Bureau of Labor Statistics). The government projections showing graphic design nearly flat while the problem-solving work grows.
  • Alex Williams, Building a UX ROI Case That Survives the Boardroom (Smashing Magazine). On why the designers who stay can show their work moved a real number.

The fundamentals were always the job

  • State of UX Hiring Report (UX Design Institute). Research across 500-plus hiring managers finding that the portfolio and the thinking matter more than the credential.
  • Jessica S. Hall, Don’t Want to Be an Order Taker? Stop Taking Orders (Hallway). On proposing a direction instead of waiting to be told what to do.
  • Kate Moran, Raluca Budiu, and Sarah Gibbons, State of UX (Nielsen Norman Group). On the fundamentals holding while the stakes rise, and strategic problem solving winning out over deliverables.
  • Jakob Nielsen, Predictions for 2026. On the bottleneck moving to judgment once AI handles execution.
  • Christine Haskell, Broken Succession. On how production gets easier while judgment gets more valuable in every one of these shifts.
